<reason>B won on the structure of the motion. Because the proposition is conjunctive, B's scope move — that A's involuntariness attack never touches the pension/sickness/injury/parental branch — stood up: A's only counters were a funding objection that B answered with a concrete levy design when directly pressed (proper A1), and a weak "the record is decoration" line that B punished in the close (you cannot credit contributions without the earnings record). B also answered both pressure questions squarely with conventional UI machinery (partial-earnings offsets for the multi-app worker; no experience-rating, so no account-charging problem), and its weighing frame — imperfect coverage versus total invisibility, plus the closing reframe that A's reclassification remedy itself presupposes standardized earnings records — survived the exchange. A was rhetorically sharper and landed real hits: the "fix for both problems"/thermometer tension, the downranking-versus-deactivation gap, the taxpayer cost-shift turn, and the foreclosure argument ("we pay the levy, so we're not employers"), which B never squarely answered. But A's strongest points remained contestable assertions, its alternative was partly converted into a dependency on the motion's own mechanism, and it under-contested half the motion. B's two clipped turns are a genuine execution cost that keeps this competitive rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange ran from B's Q2 (name a better arrangement for the starved worker) to A's Rebuttal 2 answer (enforce classification where control exists, arguing the contractor track forecloses it) to B's closing reframe (reclassification presupposes the very earnings records the motion mandates, then adds years of litigation) — which turned A's demanded alternative into a dependency, though A's foreclosure counter and "not a floor, a ceiling" rejoinder kept the branch contested.</best_rebuttal>
